resetHelp.title: Reset your password
resetHelp.intro: OTW runs on your own server: there is no mailbox to send a reset link to, and no unauthenticated way in. Reset the password from a terminal on the machine that hosts it.
resetHelp.step.shell: Open a shell on the machine running OTW.
resetHelp.step.run: Run this, with your account name in place of USERNAME. It prints a one-time password.
resetHelp.step.signIn: Sign in with that password. The app asks you for a new one straight away.
resetHelp.ownPassword: Rather choose the password yourself? Pipe it in: never pass it as an argument, a process's command line is readable on the host.
resetHelp.renamed: Container named differently? List them and use the core one.
resetHelp.note.sessions: A reset signs out every device.
resetHelp.note.data: Nothing is lost: the vault and stored provider keys are sealed with OTW_SECRET_KEY, not with your password.
resetHelp.note.bare: Not running Docker? Run the otw-core binary with the same arguments and DATABASE_URL set.

settings.network.lanHttpsHelp: Uses a free Let's Encrypt certificate obtained through your DNS provider (DNS challenge), so it works on a private network without opening any port. DuckDNS is free: sign in at duckdns.org, create a subdomain, and paste its token below.

settings.backup.title: Backup database
settings.backup.intro: Run this on the host where the stack is deployed. It dumps the whole database over the existing Postgres connection: no extra access required.
settings.backup.encryptBody: A dump contains your data in the clear. Pipe it through gpg (or age) so the file is encrypted on disk; you'll be prompted for a passphrase.
settings.backup.security1: API keys/credentials (news feeds, data providers) are already encrypted at rest with OTW_SECRET_KEY, so they appear only as ciphertext in the dump. The backup is useless for those without that key.
settings.backup.security2: Back up OTW_SECRET_KEY (from your .env) separately (not inside the same dump), or encrypted secrets can't be restored.
settings.backup.security3: The dump includes live sessions tokens. Treat the file as a secret, or drop that table after restoring and sign in again.
settings.backup.security4: Store the encrypted backup off-box and rotate older copies.
settings.update.title: Update app
settings.update.intro: Updating rebuilds the containers, which the app can't do to itself by design: it runs without shell or Docker access to keep the attack surface small. Run these on the host:
settings.update.before1: Take a database backup first (see the Backup section).
settings.update.before2: Migrations run automatically on the new container's first boot.
settings.update.before3: Review release notes for any breaking changes.

settings.mcp.subtitle: Lets AI agents (any MCP-compatible client) use this app through a controlled gateway. Each token decides which modules an agent can read or change; everything else stays out of reach. Account, network, secrets and data-wipe operations are never exposed.
settings.mcp.offNote: The MCP endpoint is off. You can prepare tokens below, but every agent request is rejected until you enable it.
settings.mcp.tokensHint: One token per agent or use case. The token is stored hashed and shown only once; revoke it any time.
settings.mcp.expiryHint: An expired token stops working everywhere, including for the in-app agent. Create a new one to replace it.
settings.mcp.name: Name
settings.mcp.createdBody: Copy the token now: it is shown only once and stored hashed.
settings.mcp.connectHint: The endpoint speaks MCP over Streamable HTTP, so any compliant client works. Authenticate with a Bearer token created above; replace <TOKEN> in the snippet.

settings.mcp.note2: Writes require the module’s read+write level; reads require at least read.
settings.mcp.note3: If the app is reachable only on localhost, agents must run on this machine too.

mailbox.setup.gmail: Turn on 2-Step Verification first: Google only offers app passwords once it is on. Paste the 16-character password without its spaces and use your full address as the username. On a Workspace account an admin can have disabled both IMAP and app passwords.
mailbox.setup.icloud: Two-factor authentication is required. Create an app-specific password on account.apple.com (Sign-In and Security → App-Specific Passwords) and sign in with your primary Apple ID address, not an alias.
mailbox.setup.yahoo: Your account password will not work here: generate an app password under Account security → Generate app password (same page for AOL).
mailbox.setup.zoho: Check the server matches your account's region: imap.zoho.eu, .com, .in or .com.au. IMAP has to be enabled in Zoho's mail settings first, and an app password is required when two-factor is on.
mailbox.setup.protonBridge: Proton Mail needs a paid plan and Bridge running on your machine; copy the address, port and Bridge password from Bridge → Settings → IMAP. Bridge's certificate is self-signed and will fail TLS verification, so choose "None": the connection never leaves your machine. And since OpenTraderWorld runs in a container, 127.0.0.1 is the container itself: point the server at the machine running Bridge, which also has to accept a connection from outside its own loopback.

automator.help.title: How the Automator works
automator.help.grid.g1: Steps run top to bottom, and inside a step the tasks run left to right. Everything runs one after another: a step groups the tasks that belong to the same moment of the workflow, it does not start them together.
automator.help.grid.g2: A task can only read what ran before it. Move a card and every reference it makes is checked again on the next save.
automator.help.grid.g3: Drag a block from the panel on the right onto a gap. The gap between two steps opens a new step, the gap between two tasks drops it into that step.
automator.help.grid.g4: The editor saves on its own a moment after each edit, and every change can be undone.
automator.help.data.d1: Each block has an id, shown at the top of its editor. A later block reads its result with {{steps.http1.output}}, and one field of it with {{steps.http1.output.items.0.name}}.
automator.help.data.d2: Readable from anywhere: {{run.started_at}}, {{run.trigger}}, {{workflow.name}}, and {{input.key}} for the values passed to a manual run.
automator.help.data.d3: Filters chain after a pipe: json, upper, lower, trim, round:2, date:"DD/MM/YYYY", default:"n/a". Only default rescues a value that is not there.
automator.help.data.d4: References are checked when the graph is saved, against the blocks that really precede it, so a broken one is refused in the editor instead of at three in the morning.
automator.help.blocks.api: Your app lists the endpoints a workflow may reach, under the blocks on the right. Search it, then click or drag one: it lands already pointed at that call. It runs only with an access token, created in Settings, AI agents, then picked in this workflow's settings.
automator.help.blocks.http: Web call reaches any URL outside the app. An address on your own network or machine is refused unless the block explicitly allows it.
automator.help.blocks.agent: AI step is one model turn, with no conversation around it. Ask for JSON when the block after it has to read fields rather than prose.
automator.help.blocks.transform: Transform reshapes what came before: pick takes one value, set builds an object, format writes a string, csv_parse reads a CSV, join folds a list into one line.
automator.help.blocks.notify: Notify sends to your channels. They are set up once in Settings, Notifications, granted to the Automator there, and only then offered here.
automator.help.blocks.delay: Wait pauses the run. Stop still answers during the wait.
automator.help.secrets.s1: A password or an API key belongs in the vault, never typed into a field. Reference it with {{vault.myvault.mykey}} in a header or a request body, the only two places it is accepted, and the resolved value is kept out of the run history.
automator.help.run.r1: Test run performs the reads and reports what a write or a send would have done, so nothing leaves the app. Run now does it for real.
automator.help.run.r2: A schedule carries its own timezone. If a run is still going when the next occurrence falls due, that occurrence is dropped rather than queued.
automator.help.fail.f1: Each task decides on its own whether to stop the run or carry on, with up to five retries and its own time limit, under Advanced in the block editor.
automator.help.fail.f2: Every run keeps one line per block with what was sent and what came back, so a failure names the block and shows the payload.
